E0828.summary: A title given to man as containing the Universal Reason, and, in the Poemander, to everything that is.
E0828.body: As Atwood reports Agrippa, man is called the Image of God because he contains the Universal Reason and corresponds with all levels of creation: “man was said to be the express Image of God, seeing he contains the Universal Reason within himself” [II.1 ¶9]. This equates the Image of God with man. In the Poemander, quoted by Atwood, the term is extended to all things: “For there is nothing which is not the Image of God” [III.3 ¶78], so the divine way proper to the Good meets one everywhere.

E0829.summary: A faculty with an elevating power, imaged by the Sphinx's 'winds', through which the phantastic spirit becomes capable of divine assimilation.
E0829.body: Atwood speaks of “the elevating power which the imagination possesses” [III.1 ¶6]. She says the Sphinx's 'winds' image this power, and through it the phantastic spirit becomes capable of divine assimilation.

E0830.summary: Atwood's phrase for what must be arrested, apparently the Protean succession of forms and colours described just before.
E0830.body: Atwood writes: “To arrest this imaginative flux of freed vitality” [III.2 ¶24]. Here 'this' apparently refers back to the Protean succession of forms and colours described just before [III.2 ¶20–22]. The flux is what the work must arrest.

E0831.summary: Impressions of the imagination that persist in a place after their act has passed and pollute its ether.
E0831.body: Atwood describes imaginative impressures that “even after their act has passed away, hang and pollute the ether of their pertinacious abode” [III.4 ¶42]. Compare the impressures implanted in the Vital Spirit (see impressures).

E0832.summary: The faculty that makes apparitions, as in dreams but more intensely.
E0832.body: Atwood: “For it is the imaginative spirit which is the maker of these images” [II.3 ¶22]. It produces the apparitions as it does in dreams, but more intensely.

E0833.summary: An operation of giving the dried matter 'drink', grinding, sealing and drying, repeated on a schedule; called the secret of the whole work.
E0833.body: In *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon*, quoted by Atwood, Imbibition gives the dried matter 'drink' (the Lion's sweat), followed by grinding, sealing and drying, repeated on a fixed schedule. The poem calls it “The secret of Imbibition never out tould;” and says “Because in it consisteth the whole subtill warke;” [III.1 ¶65]. In Eudoxus, also quoted, Imbibition is an operation named for the Red (with the citrine Mercury). In the Sixth Key it is paired with drying in the cycle of multiplication: “imbibing and drying” [IV.3 ¶16].

E0834.summary: The direct operative cause of the work, which Atwood says the alchemists concealed.
E0834.body: Atwood asks of the adepts “what was their immediate efficient?” [II.1 ¶47], meaning the direct operative cause of the work, which they concealed. Shortly after she speaks of arts and media “producing the central efficient into conscious being and effect” [II.1 ¶52]. The text does not say that the 'central efficient' and the 'immediate efficient' are the same.

E0835.summary: In Roger Bacon, as quoted, the goal that cannot be reached without a sanctified mind, purified soul and union with God.
E0835.body: Atwood quotes Roger Bacon: “it is impossible for you to attain this immortal essentiality” [III.3 ¶28] without a sanctified mind, a purified soul and union with God.

E0836.summary: Geber's list of mental defects that exclude a person from the Art.
E0836.body: Atwood introduces Geber's list: “respecting the Impediments of Mind, the Arabian continues” [III.4 ¶3]. The defects are lack of sagacity, dullness, fantasy, changeability, beast-like blindness, disbelief and love of money. Each excludes a person from the work.

E0837.summary: What mesmeric tests identify as the same throughout; not further defined.
E0837.body: Atwood says such tests “prove nothing but to identify the same Imponderable through all” [II.2 ¶7]. The text does not define the term further here.

E0838.summary: Imaginative impressions implanted in the Vital Spirit by birth into sense, which cloud the spirit and obscure intelligence.
E0838.body: Atwood speaks of “imaginative impressures which, by the birth into sense, had become implanted there” [II.2 ¶8], that is, in the Vital Spirit, where they obscure intelligence. They are residual: “their impressure yet remains” [II.2 ¶10]. The spirit may “err amongst the turbulent and shadowy impressures of this of this life’s birth and sphere of accidents” [II.2 ¶14]. Compare imaginative impressures, which pollute a place [III.4 ¶42].

E0839.summary: In the Poemander, that which contains all things, being most capacious, swift and powerful.
E0839.body: Atwood quotes the Poemander: “Consider that which contains all things” [III.3 ¶78]. It is described thus: “it is most capacious, most swift, and most strong” [III.3 ¶78].

E0840.summary: Being without body, whose necessary existence Aristotle demonstrates; glossed as essential being.
E0840.body: Atwood refers to Aristotle demonstrating the necessary existence of “incorporeal (i.e., essential) being” [II.1 ¶37]. She glosses incorporeal being as essential being.

E0841.summary: In Aliphili, as quoted, the action of the fiery water on fixed gold, reducing it to black earth.
E0841.body: Atwood quotes Aliphili: the fiery water “incrudates even the mature, constant, and very fixed, fiery and abiding mass and matter of gold” [II.1 ¶14], reducing it to black earth.

E0842.summary: The Matter as formless subject opposed to form, apprehended only by the Indefinite; not to be despised when turned towards things prior.
E0842.body: In a summary drawn from Plotinus and Porphyry, which Atwood endorses, the Indefinite is the Matter as the formless subject opposed to form. Yet “This Indefinite is not therefore everywhere to be despised” [III.2 ¶49] when it applies itself to things prior, that is, the divine exemplaries and the most excellent life. Plotinus, as quoted, adds that by the principle that like knows like, “the Indefinite also will be apprehended by the Indefinite” [III.2 ¶53]. Reason then passes out into an undefined void of thought. Compare Infinite.

E0843.summary: Atwood's account from Norton: provisional instruments are used at first until the determinate ones prove themselves fit by the Spirit.
E0843.body: Atwood, giving what she says Norton shows: “indeterminate instruments must be employed in the beginning, until the determinate shall declare themselves as by the Spirit they are proved fit” [III.4 ¶40]. Compare Vaughan's indeterminate agents [III.4 ¶44].

E0844.summary: Vaughan's advice to use agents provisionally until a single determinate agent is found.
E0844.body: Atwood quotes Vaughan: “Make use of indeterminate agents till thou canst find a determinate one” [III.4 ¶44]. The agents are not further defined. Compare indeterminate / determinate instruments [III.4 ¶40].

forms: individuals of various ages and nations, whose names are renowned in philosophy
E0845.summary: Atwood's description of the witnesses gathered in the Inquiry, many of whom attest the Stone from personal experience.
E0845.body: Atwood uses this phrase for the witnesses she has gathered for the Inquiry, many of whom attest the Stone from personal experience [IV.4 ¶2]. She relies on them as support.

E0846.summary: The outward method that moves away from the causal source and cannot originate effects (Appendix).
E0846.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes something that “the inductive philosophy or method never can arrive at, since it goes further and further out, and finds its strength in remoteness from the causal source” [APP ¶120]. The method cannot originate effects. Compare inductive sciences [III.1 ¶8].

E0847.summary: The modern experimental sciences, which Atwood criticizes because their long-accumulated facts fail to satisfy reason.
E0847.body: Atwood criticizes the inductive sciences and the modern method of experimenting. Facts accumulated over ages have not yielded the satisfaction reason requires [III.1 ¶8]. Compare inductive philosophy [APP ¶120].

E0848.summary: The lower region of life where the Sulphur lies bound (Appendix).
E0848.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of the Sulphur as “bound down in the inferior mineral region of life” [APP ¶125]. Compare Infernal life, which also represents the Mineral Kingdom [APP ¶33].

E0849.summary: The voluntary agent in life, representing the Mineral Kingdom and residing in man in the lumbar region (Appendix).
E0849.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says: “The Infernal is the voluntary agent in life, and represents the Mineral Kingdom.” [APP ¶33]. In man it resides in the lumbar region. Compare Infernal motive wheel [III.1 ¶60].

E0850.summary: The swifter contrary current in the circulation, which surmounts and eclipses the Divine Light.
E0850.body: Atwood: “the swifter current of the Infernal motive wheel surmounts and eclipses the Divine Light in the circulation” [III.1 ¶60].

E0851.summary: Fashionable faithlessness that denounces whatever is new without rational ground; Atwood calls it perhaps the most absurd obstacle to human advancement.
E0851.body: Atwood defines it: “by infidelity, we mean that fashionable kind of faithlessness, which, without rational foundation, denounces everything that is new” [III.4 ¶12]. It also denounces whatever is unfamiliar and believes nothing worthy of belief or veneration. She calls it perhaps the most absurd obstacle to human advancement.

E0852.summary: What the Matter is, 'a certain Infinity', which eludes thought as a circumscribing boundary.
E0852.body: Atwood says the Matter is “but a certain Infinity” [III.2 ¶53], and that “for the thought, as circumscribing boundary, eludes the Infinite” [III.2 ¶57]. Compare Indefinite [III.2 ¶49, ¶53].

E0853.summary: A name for the Mysteries, as the beginning of a life of reason and virtue.
E0853.body: Atwood reports the view of the Platonist, Psellus and Cicero that the Mysteries “were truly called Initia, for they were the beginning of a life of reason and virtue” [II.2 ¶4].

E0854.summary: The origin to which life is led back from created individuality, described as its return to its First Source.
E0854.body: Atwood describes life being led “from the manifest created individuality, back into the Initial germ” [III.3 ¶79]. There it “returns to refund its treasury again its First Source” [III.3 ¶79]. The Initial germ is thus linked to the First Source. Compare Initial Source and Initial Principle.

E0855.summary: The first principle on which the whole Hermetic philosophy and occult tradition depend; named variously by the philosophers, and Wisdom or Supreme Crown in the Zohar.
E0855.body: Atwood says the whole Hermetic philosophy and every tradition of occult science depend on this principle: “it will be requisite to consider this, their Initial Principle, more particularly” [III.1 ¶3]. She proposes to examine how it may have become known 'in its first arcane descent and emanation'. What 'this' refers back to is not clear from the record. In the Zohar, once it has become manifest, it “is in the Zohar designated by the name of Wisdom, or the Supreme Crown” [III.2 ¶3], and “the divine hypostasis is distinguished by the epithet of Unknown” [III.2 ¶3]. This equates it with Wisdom, the Supreme Crown and the Unknown in the Beginning. Atwood surveys the philosophers: “some saying indeed of the Initial Principle, that it is one and finite, others infinite” [III.2 ¶35]. Some, “as Heraclitus, according to essence, have denominated it to be fire” [III.2 ¶35]. Another, “rather regarding the perfection and origin of the One Thing in consciousness, calls it Intellect” [III.2 ¶35]. Others call it water or earth. She concludes that “the substance alluded to by them all is the same” [III.2 ¶34], with mind and matter consubstantial in it.

E0856.summary: Nature's origin, into which she was followed and where she works her own annihilation and survives on her redeemed Light.
E0856.body: Atwood speaks of the effort “to follow mysterious Nature through many intricate windings and circumstantial difficulties, into her Initial Source” [IV.4 ¶6]. There Nature voluntarily works her own annihilation and survives upon her redeemed Light. Compare Initial germ [III.3 ¶79].

E0857.summary: The Initiated knew the means of the Art and kept silent about them; initiation is admission into the deeper mysteries.
E0857.body: Atwood notes “that the Initiated were so profoundly silent upon these means” [II.1 ¶53], meaning the means of the Art. Atwood also quotes Iamblicus and Synesius on initiation as admission into the deeper mysteries. Restoration of the soul is obtained by a few 'as a gift of divinity and initiation'. The uninitiated, “those who have not been purely initiated” [II.2 ¶11], are surrounded by 'dense thickets'. Compare Initia [II.2 ¶4].
